Seminar Title:

Structure stabilization and interface engineering of Mn and Co-free Ni-rich layered oxide cathodes via site-specific doping in lithium-ion batteries

Seminar Type:

Defence Seminar

Department:

Ceramic Engineering

Speaker Name:

Abhishek Kumar ( Rollno : 519cr1003)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

Meeting room, Ceramic Engineering (hybrid mode, MS Team code: x6Up9t)

Date and Time:

13 Nov 2026 4 PM

Contact:

Partha Saha

Abstract:

The demand for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), particularly for electric vehicles and portable electronics, has spurred renewed interest and extensive research on Ni-rich layered oxide cathodes such as LixNiyMnzCo1-y-zO2 (NMC). The NMC-based cathodes offer high specific capacities (~180&ndash220 mAh g⁻&sup1) and operating voltages of ~3.6&ndash3.7 V, but their practical use is hindered by severe Li⁺/Ni&sup2⁺ cation mixing, irreversible H2&rarrH3 phase transitions during high-voltage cycling (&le 4.5 V), oxygen instability, and rapid capacity and voltage fading. Moreover, reliance on cobalt and manganese raises concerns related to cost, supply-chain vulnerability, toxicity, and transition-metal dissolution. To address these challenges, a systematic materials-design strategy has been explored to enhance the structural stability, electrochemical performance, and sustainability of Ni-rich layered oxide cathodes. The work focuses on three interconnected approaches: (i) site-specific cation doping to stabilize conventional NMC cathodes, (ii) development of cobalt- and manganese-free Ni-rich layered oxides, and (iii) functional separator and interface engineering to mitigate cathode-electrolyte degradation. To stabilize conventional NMC compositions, dual-site doping using Mg&sup2⁺ at lithium (3a) sites and Zr⁴⁺ at transition-metal (preferentially Ni, 3b) sites was exploited in LiNi₀.₆₅Mn₀.₁₀Co₀.₂₅O₂ (NMC6525) to suppress cation disorder and strengthen the transition-metal&ndashoxygen framework. Building on this concept, a cobalt-free cathode LixNi0.8Mn0.1Mg0.1O2 (NMM811) and ultrahigh Ni-rich Co-/Mn-free cathodes LiNi0.95Mn0.025Mg0.025O2 (NMM95) and LiNi0.95Zr0.025Mg0.025O2 (NZM95) were developed. Comprehensive structural, microscopic, spectroscopic, and electrochemical analyses demonstrate that Zr/Mg co-doping reduces Li+/Ni2+ mixing from ~11% to ~2.9%, enlarges interlayer spacing, strengthens Ni&ndashO bonding, and suppresses oxygen migration and rock-salt phase formation. These effects inhibit the H2&rarrH3 transition, yielding ~85% capacity retention with a low voltage-fading rate (~0.12 mV cycle⁻&sup1) after 200 cycles. The cobalt-free NMM95 and Co-/Mn-free NZM95 cathodes retain ~71% and ~78% capacity, respectively, after 200 cycles, outperforming Co-containing NMC95 (~60%). Synchrotron-based X-ray absorption near-edge structure analysis reveals that reduced oxygen-related defects and enhanced Ni&ndashO bond strength contribute to improved electrochemical performance. Furthermore, integration of NZM95 with a polarized &beta-phase PVDF-HFP nanofiber-coated separator stabilizes the cathode&ndashelectrolyte interface by regulating ion solvation and suppressing parasitic reactions, enabling ~215 mAh g&minus1 with ~86% retention after 200 cycles, compared with ~207 mAh g&minus1 and ~78% retention using a conventional PP separator. Overall, this work establishes an integrated pathway combining dopant engineering, Co/Mn elimination, and ferroelectric separator/electrode interface design, realizing stable, high-voltage, and sustainable Ni-rich cathodes for next-generation LIBs.
